newsitem.title: USA: Funds probe to continue, after dramatic start.
newsitem.headline: Funds probe to continue, after dramatic start.

text.p: A Senate probe into political fund-raising scandals is set to continue on Wednesday with testimony from Richard Sullivan, former finance director for the Democratic National Commitee, after a dramatic start on Tuesday.
Partisan sniping marked the first day of the long-awaited, televised hearings by the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, despite public assurances of cooperation and fairness.

Chairman Fred Thompson of Tennessee, who sharpened his prosecutorial skills as Republican counsel during the Senate Watergate hearings two decades ago, went on the offensive immediately with an allegation that China planned to buy its way into American politics.
Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the ranking Democrat on the panel, also dropped a bombshell when he revealed a surprise offer of testimony by a key player in the tangled web of donations, John Huang.
Huang's lawyer said Huang agreed to speak "truthfully to the best of his knowledge and honest recollection" if given limited immunity from prosecution.
Ty Cobb told public television on Tuesday that Huang would deny under oath that he was an agent for China or any other government.
"Mr. Huang did not commit espionage, and he's confident of that fact," Cobb said. "He would like to face those allegations, confront them and dispel them."
ABC said it had learned that Huang would deny any wrongdoing by the president.

As night fell on Washington and the hearings ended for the day, players on both sides were expressing concern that the highly publicized hearings might deter Congress from enacting long-overdue campaign finance reforms.
"We will wind up at the end of this year having left the system that bred these illegalities in place," Glenn told public television's "NewsHour with Jim Lehrer." "Let's go after this whole system."

His comments were echoed by Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican and the co-author of legislation backed by President Bill Clinton that would ban so-called "soft money" contributions, unlimited donations that are theoretically designated for political parties rather than individual candidates.
In practice, those funds are often used to further individual candidates' campaigns.
"If we do not clean up this system, I fear for the future of the electoral process," McCain told CNN.
Senate Democrats sent a letter the Majority Leader Trent Lott, urging him to accelerate attention to campaign fund-raising reforms.
"Elections are too long, too negative and too expensive," they wrote in the letter. "The American people want us to clean up the system, and they want us to do it now."
The Democrats asked the Mississippi Republican to announce a specific date to bring campaign finance reform measures to the floor.

Apart from foreign influence, the panel over the next four weeks will examine reports of sleepovers in the White House's Lincoln Bedroom for campaign high rollers, alleged calls to solicit funds made from the White House by Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, and Gore's attendance at a fund raiser in a Buddhist temple with monks who had taken a vow of poverty.

Senators of both parties decried the bending of campaign finance laws in the last elections. The more than $600 million spent in the 1996 congressional and presidential campaigns -- nearly 50 percent more than the 1991-92 cycle -- broke all records.

Huang is a central figure in the investigation of domestic and foreign contributions, and his offer to testify will be considered, Thompson said, if he wants to give "full, complete and truthful" testimony.
